newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian voters desert Hanson in home electorate.
newsitem.headline: Australian voters desert Hanson in home electorate.

text.p: Australian voters are deserting race row politician Pauline Hanson in her own electorate and could evict her from parliament if a general election were held now, a new opinion poll showed on Monday.

In contrast to national polls showing rising support for Hanson's far right One Nation party, The Bulletin news magazine's survey showed support for Hanson in her electorate had slipped more than 10 percent since the March 1996 election.

The Bulletin poll gave Hanson 36 percent of the vote in her electorate of Oxley, in the conservative state of Queensland, compared with a thumping 48.6 percent in March 1996, when she stole the seat from the then ruling Labor party.
Labor lost the national election to the Liberal-National coalition, ending 13 years of Labor rule.
The Bulletin poll, if reflected at the next election, would force Hanson to rely on Liberal party voters to retain her seat. In Australia, voters rank candidates in order of preference.
"She could still lose her own seat at the next election if the two major parties stood together to deny her preferences," The Bulletin said in a commentary on the survey.
The Liberal and Labor parties have tentatively agreed to do this at the next election, it reported. A general election is not due until early 1999.
Despite Hanson's fragility, a separate poll confirmed strong national support for her One Nation party, The Bulletin said.
One Nation opposes further immigration from Asia, wants Aboriginal welfare cut back and supports moves to overturn a national ban on semi-automatic rifles and shotguns.

Thirty-five percent of voters, including those who would give the ruling coalition conservative parties or Labor their first preference, believe the One Nation movement has been "a good thing overall for Australia", the magazine said.
"A similar proportion believe (Prime Minister) John Howard, rather than ignore or confront her, should consider her policies and the reasons why some people support them," it said.
In earlier opinion polls, One Nation has outpolled the third major party, the Australian Democrats, as support for Howard's government has fallen to its lowest level since it won office.
The polls come against a backdrop of violent protests against meetings of One Nation party, launched three weeks ago by Hanson, and a row over Aboriginal land title.
Australia's Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation, an official body seeking to harmonise black-white relations, said on Monday the two issues were threatening its work.
"The reconciliation process is at risk," council deputy chairman Ian Viner, a Liberal party member and former Aboriginal affairs minister, said after a council meeting in Melbourne.
